   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT

  MEMORANDUM

  TO:  Commission Standardization Ad Hoc Committee Liaisons

  FROM:  Michael Forbes, Director of Community Development
  Nestor Otazu, Deputy Director of Rent Stabilization
  Cameron Kesinger, Senior Management Analyst

  DATE:  May 14, 2024

  SUBJECT:  Overview of Rent Stabilization Commission

INTRODUCTION

This report is intended to provide a brief overview of the Rent Stabilization Commission (RSC) and
its activities since its inception in 2019.

BACKGROUND

Between 2016 and 2019, Community Development Department staff and community partners
conducted studies, outreach events, and facilitated sessions to seek feedback from the community
on potential revisions to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance.

This outreach resulted in a variety of recommendations for revisions to the ordinance. Several of the
recommended revisions were approved by the City Council through a series of ordinances, including
extending Just Cause Eviction protections for Chapter 6 tenants and revising the calculations for
allowable rent increases. The City Council determined that some of the recommended ordinance
revisions were best discussed and resolved with the assistance and feedback of a commission that
represented the interests of various community stakeholders.

On April 2, 2019, the City Council adopted an ordinance establishing the RSC, comprised of an equal
number of landlords, tenants, and at-large residents, to act as an advisory body to the Council on all
matters related to the Rent Stabilization Ordinance. Per the Beverly Hills Municipal Code, the RSC
has the authority to 1) make recommendations to the City Council concerning amendments to
Chapter 5 and 6 of Title 5 that have not been resolved by the City Council and 2) perform any other
functions that may be designated by resolution or motion of the City Council.

The City Council charged the RSC with discussing the following topics related to the Rent
Stabilization Ordinance:

  1. Modification to the Major Remodel eviction category, which permitted tenants to be evicted
  for certain major remodeling projects meeting a minimum dollar threshold
   2. Regulations regarding the Cash for Keys process, through which landlords attempt to
  negotiate with tenants for a voluntary vacancy arrangement

  3. Evaluation of relocation fee amounts where tenants are evicted for any No Fault reason

  4. Review of habitability standards and the implementation of a proactive inspection program
  for every rental unit

  5. Review of allowable pass-through surcharges for Chapter 5 and 6 tenants, through which
  landlords are able to charge tenants for various items including refuse fees and the Rent
  Stabilization Administration Fee

  6. Review of the Landlord Tenant Handbook, which landlords are required to provide to every
  new tenant at least 24 hours prior to the tenant’s execution of the lease

DISCUSSION

The RSC held its first meeting in June 2020. Over the past four years, the Commission has
thoughtfully discussed each of the topics as charged by the Council and has approved resolutions to
memorialize its recommendations. One of these recommendations, the modification of the Major
Remodel eviction category, was ultimately adopted by the City Council. The Landlord Tenant
Handbook was reviewed and revised per the RSC’s recommendations. RSC resolutions that reflect
the RSC’s recommendations for the remaining topics have been completed, and the RSC’s
recommendations on these topics are pending further consideration by the Liaisons and City Council.

With consideration of these topics as originally directed by the City Council completed, the RSC does
not currently have specific matters to discuss or business to conduct. The RSC does not serve as a
hearing body for any applications, appeals, or processes of the Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The
Municipal Code charges a hearing officer with the authority to consider Registered Rent Appeals,
Certified Rent Appeals, and Landlord Rent Adjustment Applications; while a City Council
subcommittee appointed by the Mayor is charged with considering Disruptive Tenant Applications.

FISCAL IMPACT

Staff resources are required to support the RSC and its monthly meetings including administering
and broadcasting meetings, and preparing meeting agendas and minutes, staff reports, and
resolutions.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the Commission Standardization Liaison Committee provide direction regarding
the RSC.

   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  CITY CLERK’S OFFICE

  MEMORANDUM

 TO:  Commission Standardization Ad Hoc Committee Liaisons

 FROM:  Huma Ahmed, City Clerk
  Michelle Ramos-Vergara, Deputy City Clerk
  Abbey Tenn, Principal Performance Auditor

 DATE:  May 14, 2024

 SUBJECT:  Discussion of Commission Recruitment Challenges

INTRODUCTION

The City’s Commissions are made up of local Beverly Hills residents (with certain exceptions)
who all volunteer their time to assist the City Council in an advisory capacity. There are currently
12 active commissions in the City of Beverly Hills.

Commissioners serve at the pleasure of the City Council and per the Commissioners’ Handbook
may “be removed from office at any time by the majority vote of the Council.” Currently, there are
multiple commission recruitments to fill vacancies that are both scheduled and unscheduled for
July 2024 and January 2025.

    Architectural Commission: One Vacancy
    Arts and Culture Commission: One Vacancy
    Charitable Solicitations Commission: One Vacancy
    Cultural Heritage Commission: Two Vacancies
    Health and Safety Commission: One Vacancy
    Traffic and Parking Commission: One Vacancy
    Rent Stabilization Commission: Five Vacancies – (recruitments on hold)

The City Clerk’s Office has repeatedly advertised the above commission vacancies in the three
locally adjudicated newspapers - the Beverly Hills Courier, the Beverly Hills Weekly, and the
Beverly Press. Additionally, commission vacancies have been advertised through e-notices,
Team Beverly Hills and the Beverly Hills Farmer’s Market, and on the City’s Instagram and
Facebook pages.

In light of the challenges experienced thus far, the City Clerk’s Office would like to request the
Commission Standardization Ad Hoc Committee Liaisons (Liaisons), Vice Mayor Sharona R.
Nazarian, PsyD and Councilmember Craig Corman review and provide feedback on this matter.
 DISCUSSION

Commissioner Terms

Commissioners are appointed by the City Council for an initial two-year term and may be
reappointed for an additional four years at the discretion of the City Council (aside from the Rent
Stabilization Commission). Rent Stabilization Commissioners are appointed for an initial four-
years, and then may seek reappointment for another four-years.

Unless noted, in some cases, all applicants must be 1) residents of the City and 2) should have
a residency in Beverly Hills for a minimum of two years.

Appointees who have served two (2) successive terms shall not be eligible for reappointment to
the same Commission. A member may serve beyond expiration of that member’s term until such
time a successor is appointed. A Commissioner must wait one year after the end of the
Commissioner’s term before applying to another Commission other than the Planning
Commission.

When vacancies occur on any of the City Commissions, they may either be scheduled or
unscheduled. Scheduled vacancies happen when a current Commissioner’s term has expired.
Unscheduled openings occur for any reason, other than the expiration of a term (e.g., illness or
change of residency). Beginning with the notification period, it usually takes about six months to
fill a vacant seat.

Application Process

Currently, the application process is as follows:

    Applicants may apply to only one (1) Commission per application cycle.
    A Commissioner must wait one year after finishing their term to be able to apply to another
  Commission, except the Planning Commission.
    An existing Commissioner may not apply to join another Commission during their term,
  unless applying for the Planning Commission.
    Commissioner appointments shall be held bi-annually in either January or July.

FISCAL IMPACT

None
RECOMMENDATION

Staff respectfully requests the Liaisons review and provide feedback on:

  1. Shall there be a one-time exemption for applicants to apply to two or more commissions
  during this recruitment cycle; or
  2. Shall the City Clerk continue to request - with City Council approval - an extension of terms
  for commissioner seats which have yet to be formally filled (on an as needed basis).

CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS
  455 North Rexford Drive
  Beverly Hills, CA 90210
  Video Teleconference
  Beverly Hills City Council Liaison / Commission Standardization Ad Hoc
  Committee Meeting

  SPECIAL MEETING HIGHLIGHTS

  Tuesday, May 14, 2024
  1:00 PM

MEETING CALLED TO ORDER
Date / Time:  May 14, 2024 / 1:08 PM
IN ATTENDANCE:  Vice Mayor Sharona Nazarian, Councilmember Craig Corman, Assistant
  City Manager Ryan Gohlich, City Clerk Huma Ahmed, Director of
  Community Development Michael Forbes

  1) Public Comment:
  a. Mark Elliot via Zoom: For point 2 he argues for the elimination of the rent
  stabilization commission and that the commission was “cynically used by the
  council” to handle things like relocation fees and terminations. He also says that
  the commissioners were disconnected from the community which prevented the
  landlords and tenants of the city from connecting with who is supposed to
  ostensibly represent them on the commission. For point 3 he attributes the failure
  to recruit commissioners to the low level of public engagement with the city
  government. He states that city hall has been extremely poor at connecting with
  residents and generating local engagement.
  b. Steve Meyer via Zoom: Echoes Mark’s comments about point 2, and states that it
  was landlord dominated with the commission usually siding with landlords. For
  point two he reflects Mark’s comments about low civic engagement, but he adds
  that prospective commissioners did not simply want to be a rubber stamp for City
  staff and instead wanted to discuss details but were given 500+ page reports on
  issues. In addition, prospective commissioners are deterred due to public scrutiny
  for virtually no benefit.

  2) Overview of Rent Stabilization Commission Activities:
  a. Presentation by Michael Forbes:
  i. From 2016-2019 there was a community outreach effort by the city to look
  at the City’s rent stabilization ordinance and see if any changes were
  necessary.
  ii. Some of these recommendations to change the ordinance were
  implemented in 2019.
  iii. Other recommendations were recommended to be studied further by a
  group consisting of both tenants and landlords, and so founded the rent
  stabilization committee to undertake this task.
 Highlights for May 14, 2024
Commission Standardization Ad Hoc Committee

  iv. In 2023, the commission concluded all the studies that council tasked them
  with and adopted a series of resolutions with recommendations to the
  liaisons and council for changes to the rent stabilization ordinance.
  v. During the COVID Pandemic the commission was tasked with serving as a
  hearing body under an emergency ordinance, which has since sunsetted.
  vi. Hearing appeals and tenant-landlord issues are handed via a hearing
  officer.
  vii. The commission currently has no business before it.
  b.  For property improvements the commission determined that it be a 50/50 pass
  through to the tenants, which includes retrofitting. These recommendations are
  planned to go before the council later this year.
  c.  As of July 1st, the commission will have 5 vacancies.
  d.  The way the commission was structured was to have three groups, tenant
  representatives, landlord representatives, and at large representatives. If 2
  members of one of the three groups was absent, the commission did not have a
  quorum.
  e.  The city clerk has recruited twice for the at large commission and has received
  zero applications.
  f.  Due to the number of vacancies, on July 1st the commission will permanently not
  have a quorum.
  g.  Both Vice Mayor Nazarian and Councilmember Corman are in favor of
  recommending to council that the commission be sunset.
  h.  Disruptive tenant hearings are required to be heard by an appointed body which
  includes two councilmembers instead of a commissioner.
  i.  Should the Committee be sunset, changes will need to be made to the ordinance
  for disruptive tenants.
  j.  The disruptive tenant ordinance was added during the pandemic.
  k.  Both Liaisons recommend sunsetting the commission
  l.  Vice Mayor Nazarian also recommends that the disruptive tenant process be
  moved from being handled by 2 councilmembers to a Public Hearing Officer.

  3) Discussion of Commission Recruitment Challenges:
  a. Presentation by Huma Ahmed:
  i. There are several commissions with scheduled and unscheduled
  vacancies for July 2024 and January 2025. These commissions are as
  follows.
  1. Architectural Commission: 1 vacancy
  2. Arts & Culture commission: 1 vacancy
  3. Charitable solicitations Commission: 1 vacancy
  4. Cultural Heritage Commission: 2 vacancies
  5. Health & Safety Commission: 1 vacancy
  6. Traffic & Parking commission: 1 vacancy
  7. Rent Stabilization Commission: 5 vacancies (recruitments on hold)
  ii. Recruitment efforts have been made to fill these vacancies; however, the
  city is not receiving applications for the positions.
  iii. City staff is planning on bringing measures that authorize temporary
  extensions for commissioners to keep the commission at a quorum.
 Highlights for May 14, 2024
Commission Standardization Ad Hoc Committee

  iv. Advertisements for the positions have been done through the three local
  newspapers, e-notices, Team BH, the Farmer’s Market, and through social
  media.
  v. Most applicants learn about the opening through either word of mouth or
  social media.
  vi. Typically, applicants must be residents of the city and have lived here for
  two years, but there are certain exceptions.
  vii. Aside from Rent Stabilization Commissioners, Commissioners are
  appointed for two-year terms and may be reappointed for an additional four
  years at the Council’s discretion.
  viii. The Clerk’s office is considering requesting a one-time exemption to allow
  commissioners to serve on more than one commission due to the low
  number of applicants.
  b.  There has been a noticeable drop in commissioner applications after the
  pandemic, which the City Clerk attributes to people reevaluating what is important
  in their lives and being less willing to take on a volunteer position that comes with
  as much work and scrutiny as a commissioner.
  c.  For the commissioners who are choosing not to renew, the reasons they gave were
  either that they were moving out of the city or that the position was too much of a
  time commitment.
  d.  There were some complaints about how personal the background checks were,
  particularly with divorce and bankruptcy history.
  e.  There also have been several times where entire groups of applicants were
  rejected due to either not being qualified for the commission or for not knowing
  basic information about the commission they were applying for.
  f.  Both liaisons are in favor of granting the one-time exemption to allow
  commissioners to be on multiple commissions as well as extensions for sitting
  commissioners to allow for additional time to recruit.
  g.  Councilmember Corman is in favor of potentially sunsetting more rubber stamp
  commissions such as Charitable Solicitations and potentially consolidating
  commission such as Human Relations and Health & Safety into a single
  commission to make sitting on them more meaningful, which would attract
  commissioners.

  4) Adjournment:
  Date / Time: May 14, 2024 / 1:54 PM
